sounds.name: First Note
sounds.ref: Classic technique: the smallest patch that plays from the keys
sounds.blurb: One oscillator, played from the keyboard and given a simple envelope: the VCS3’s “hello world”.
sounds.how: On the VCS3 nothing is connected until you place a pin. This patch uses four: Oscillator 1’s ramp into the envelope shaper, the shaped signal to both outputs, and the keyboard’s voltage to Oscillator 1’s frequency. The envelope starts out repeating on its own, as a VCS3 envelope does; turning OFF past 6 makes it wait for a key, so each note starts and stops like a normal synth.

steps.title: Oscillator 1 through the envelope
steps.why:
The first pins: Oscillator 1’s ramp (row 2) into the envelope shaper (column D), and the shaped signal (row 12) into columns B and C, the two output channels.
- Pins D2, B12 and C12.
- Oscillator 1 FREQUENCY 6 (middle C), ramp LEVEL 5: the knob marked 2 sets how much reaches row 2, wherever it is pinned.
- SIGNAL LEVEL 6: the knob marked 12.
- ATTACK 0.5, ON 0, DECAY 3.5, OFF 3: the envelope runs round on its own, so you hear repeated notes without touching a key.
- OUTPUT LEVEL 8 on both: the amplifiers only open past 5.
- Listen for: a bright, buzzy note repeating about five times a second.

steps.title: Play it from the keys
steps.why:
The keyboard is plugged into input channel 1, so its pitch is on row 8. Pin row 8 into column I and Oscillator 1 follows the keys.
- Pin I8: row 8 to Oscillator 1 frequency.
- INPUT LEVEL CHANNEL 1 at 5: one semitone per key. Lower squeezes the notes together; higher spreads them apart.
- Listen for: the repeating note changes pitch with each key, but still never stops.

steps.title: Make the envelope wait for a key
steps.why:
Turn OFF past 6 and the envelope stops after each fall and waits. Now each key starts one note, which holds while the key is down and fades when you let go.
- OFF 10: manual.
- Listen for: separate notes, each with a short tail, and silence between them.

context.osc1.ramp: In this sound: how loud the oscillator is going into the envelope shaper. Very high levels can make the shaper’s amplifier rough.
context.in.ch1: In this sound: at 5 each key is one semitone. Try 2.5 for quarter tones or 10 for whole tones.
context.env.decay: In this sound: how long each note rings after you let go. Turn up for a long fade.
context.env.off: In this sound: past 6 the envelope waits for a key. Turn it below 6 and the notes repeat on their own.
context.out1.level: In this sound: the amplifier for channel 1. Below 5 it shuts completely.

tweaks.try: Turn OFF back down to 3 and hold a key
tweaks.hear: The note repeats on its own again, several times a second.
Everything an octave and a half lower: the keyboard starts lower.

sounds.name: Swept Coloured Noise
sounds.ref: From the EMS manual — Specimen Patch 1
sounds.blurb: Noise through the filter and the repeating envelope, with three oscillators moving the decay and the filter: the manual’s first patch.
sounds.how: This is the patch the VCS3 manual walks through first, pin by pin: H7, D10, B12, C12, L2, L4, N6, O16 and P15. Noise goes through the filter and the envelope shaper to both outputs. Oscillators 1 and 2, slow and nearly in tune, beat against each other on the envelope’s decay, Oscillator 3 sweeps the filter, and the joystick rides both output levels. The knob settings are this app’s: the manual draws them as dials.

steps.title: Noise through the filter
steps.why:
Noise (row 7) into the filter (column H), and the filter (row 10) into the envelope shaper (column D).
- Pin H7: noise into the filter.
- Pin D10: the filter into the envelope shaper.
- Noise LEVEL 7, COLOUR 5: white noise, fairly hot.
- Filter FREQUENCY 7.2 (1.2 kHz) and RESPONSE 4.5: a softened, slightly peaky hiss.
- Filter LEVEL 9: the knob marked 10.
- Nothing is heard yet: the shaper’s output has not been pinned anywhere.

steps.title: A repeating envelope to both outputs
steps.why:
The shaped signal (row 12) goes to both outputs, B and C. With OFF below 6 the envelope cycles on its own, so the noise comes in bursts without any key.
- Pins B12 and C12.
- SIGNAL LEVEL 9: the knob marked 12.
- ATTACK 3, ON 2, DECAY 5, OFF 3.5: a soft rise, a short hold, a falling tail and a short rest, round and round.
- Listen for: breathing bursts of filtered noise.

steps.title: Two slow oscillators on the decay
steps.why:
Oscillator 1’s ramp (row 2) and Oscillator 2’s triangle (row 4) both go into column L, the decay time. They are slow and slightly out of tune, so they drift in and out of step and each burst has a different length.
- Pins L2 and L4.
- Oscillator 1 FREQUENCY 2 (4.4 Hz), ramp LEVEL 4; Oscillator 2 FREQUENCY 2.1, triangle LEVEL 4.
- Listen for: the bursts getting longer and shorter in a slow, uneven pattern.

steps.title: Oscillator 3 sweeps the filter
steps.why:
Oscillator 3’s triangle (row 6) into column N, the filter frequency. At this speed it is a slow sweep, the job an LFO does on other synths.
- Pin N6.
- Oscillator 3 FREQUENCY 3.5 (0.6 Hz), triangle LEVEL 5.
- Listen for: the noise rising and falling in brightness, like surf.

steps.title: The joystick on the output levels
steps.why:
The joystick’s vertical (row 16) goes to output channel 1’s level (column O) and its horizontal (row 15) to channel 2’s (column P). Move the stick and you fade and pan the sound by hand.
- Pins O16 and P15.
- RANGE 4 on both.
- OUTPUT LEVEL 7.5 on both, so the channels are open with the stick in the middle.
- Try: drag the stick right to bring up the right side, down to fade the left.

context.vcf.freq: In this sound: the centre of the sweep. Lower is a darker rumble; higher, a brighter hiss.
context.osc3.tri: In this sound: how wide the filter sweep is. Turn down for a gentle movement.
context.env.off: In this sound: the rest between bursts. Past 6 the bursts stop until you press a key.
context.osc2.freq: In this sound: tuned close to Oscillator 1 so the two beat. The further apart, the faster the pattern changes.
context.noise.colour: In this sound: the colour of the noise before the filter. Left is darker, right thinner.

tweaks.try: Drag the joystick around while it plays
tweaks.hear: The bursts move between the speakers and fade up and down.
The noise starts to whistle at the filter frequency, like wind.

sounds.name: Ring Modulator Octave
sounds.ref: From the EMS manual — the ring modulator
sounds.blurb: Two sine waves at the same pitch multiplied: the result is one note an octave up.
sounds.how: The manual’s first ring-modulator example: Oscillator 1’s sine and the filter, oscillating on its own as a second sine, both tuned to about middle C, go into the ring modulator’s two inputs (E1 and F10). A ring modulator gives the sum and the difference of its inputs: the difference of two equal pitches is nothing, so only the sum is left, an octave above. Because the two are never exactly in tune, the octave slowly swells and fades.

steps.title: Two sine sources
steps.why:
Oscillator 1 at middle C, and the filter turned into an oscillator by turning RESPONSE past 6. Nothing is pinned yet.
- Oscillator 1 FREQUENCY 6 (261.6 Hz), sine LEVEL 6.
- Filter FREQUENCY 5.2 (262 Hz), RESPONSE 7, LEVEL 6: the filter whistles its own sine at about the same pitch.

steps.title: Into the ring modulator
steps.why:
Pin E1 (Oscillator 1’s sine into input A) and F10 (the filter into input B), then the ring modulator’s output (row 13) to both outputs.
- Pins E1, F10, B13 and C13.
- Ring modulator LEVEL 7: the knob marked 13.
- Listen for: a single tone an octave above middle C, slowly swelling and fading as the two sources drift.

steps.title: Retune and listen
steps.why:
Move Oscillator 1 away from the filter’s pitch and two notes appear, the sum and the difference, moving in opposite directions. Back in tune they merge again.
- Oscillator 1 FREQUENCY 5.9: a little flat, so the sum and difference split apart and beat.
- Listen for: a lower tone sliding down and the octave sliding a little, and a slow beat between them.

context.osc1.freq: In this sound: tuned near the filter. The further away, the further apart the two ring-modulated notes.
context.vcf.response: In this sound: past 6, so the filter makes its own sine. Below 6 it stops and the ring modulator has nothing on input B.
context.vcf.freq: In this sound: the pitch of the filter’s own tone, matched to Oscillator 1.
context.ring.level: In this sound: the volume of the result.

tweaks.try: Turn the dial slowly from 5.5 to 6.5
tweaks.hear: Two notes that cross over, merge into one octave at unison, then split again.
The sine gets harmonics, so the result turns bell-like and clangy.

sounds.name: Bell Tones
sounds.ref: From the EMS manual — the ring modulator
sounds.blurb: Ring-modulated oscillators, filtered, struck by the repeating envelope and sent into the spring reverb.
sounds.how: The manual’s bell patch, with its own pins and settings: E1 F3 F4 I16 J15 H13 D10 G10 C12 B14. Oscillator 1’s sine is multiplied with both of Oscillator 2’s waves, which gives a cluster of unrelated overtones, the mark of a bell. The filter softens it, the envelope strikes it with an instant attack and a long decay, and the reverb gives it a room. The joystick retunes both oscillators. Two changes from the manual: Oscillator 2 sits a little above Oscillator 1, because two dials at the same number here give exactly the same pitch (on the hardware they never quite match), and the filter is opened a little further.

steps.title: A clangy ring modulation
steps.why:
Oscillator 1’s sine into input A, and Oscillator 2’s square and triangle together into input B.
- Pins E1, F3 and F4.
- Oscillator 1 FREQUENCY 7.5 (1.2 kHz); Oscillator 2 FREQUENCY 7.85, a little higher.
- Oscillator 1 sine LEVEL 6; Oscillator 2 square LEVEL 5 and triangle LEVEL 6.
- Ring modulator LEVEL 7.
- Not heard yet: the ring modulator’s output is not pinned to an output.

steps.title: Filter and strike it
steps.why:
The ring modulator goes through the filter (H13), the filter into the envelope shaper (D10), and the struck sound to output channel 2 (C12).
- Pins H13, D10 and C12.
- Filter FREQUENCY 8 (2.2 kHz), RESPONSE 0, LEVEL 10: a gentle top cut.
- ATTACK 0, ON 0, DECAY 6, OFF 3: an instant strike, a long ring, starting again after a short rest.
- SIGNAL LEVEL 9.
- Listen for: a bell struck again and again on the right.

steps.title: Reverb on the other side
steps.why:
The filter also feeds the reverb (G10), and the reverb comes out of channel 1 (B14). Dry bell on the right, spring room on the left.
- Pins G10 and B14.
- Reverb MIX 5, LEVEL 10.
- Listen for: the bell ringing on into a spring echo on the left.

steps.title: The joystick tunes the bell
steps.why:
The joystick’s vertical goes to Oscillator 1 (I16), its horizontal to Oscillator 2 (J15), so moving the stick retunes the cluster.
- Pins I16 and J15.
- RANGE 4 on both.
- Try: move the stick slowly while it plays. Each position is a different bell.

context.env.decay: In this sound: how long each strike rings.
context.env.off: In this sound: the rest between strikes. Past 6 it only strikes when you press a key.
context.osc2.freq: In this sound: tuned against Oscillator 1. Small changes give completely different bells.
context.vcf.freq: In this sound: how bright the bell is.
context.rev.mix: In this sound: how much spring is in the left channel.

tweaks.try: Turn OFF to 10 and play keys
tweaks.hear: One strike per key instead of a steady repeat.
The bell changes from a gong to a small chime.

sounds.name: Filter Picks Out Harmonics
sounds.ref: From the EMS manual — the filter
sounds.blurb: A low ramp wave through a sharp filter that Oscillator 3 sweeps up and down, so the harmonics ring out one by one.
sounds.how: The manual’s filter demonstration: H2, B10 and N6. A ramp wave is made of a fundamental plus every harmonic above it. A sharp filter, swept slowly, lets each harmonic through in turn, so you hear a rising and falling scale of the harmonic series over the drone. Here row 10 also goes to channel 2 (C10), so it plays on both sides.

steps.title: A low ramp through a sharp filter
steps.why:
Oscillator 1’s ramp into the filter, and the filter to both outputs.
- Pins H2, B10 and C10.
- Oscillator 1 FREQUENCY 4.5 (55 Hz), ramp LEVEL 5.
- Filter FREQUENCY 5.5, RESPONSE 5.8: just short of oscillating, so it rings sharply.
- Filter LEVEL 7.
- Listen for: a low buzz with one harmonic ringing loudly over it.

steps.title: Oscillator 3 sweeps the filter
steps.why:
Oscillator 3, as a slow ramp, moves the filter frequency (N6). Each harmonic rings out as the filter passes it.
- Pin N6.
- Oscillator 3 FREQUENCY 2 (0.12 Hz, about eight seconds a sweep), triangle LEVEL 7.
- Oscillator 3 SHAPE 0: the triangle becomes a falling ramp. The filter rises as the voltage falls, so the sweep climbs slowly and drops back at once.
- Listen for: a slow scale of harmonics climbing over the drone, then starting again.

context.vcf.response: In this sound: how sharp the filter is. Higher picks out single harmonics more clearly; past 6.6 the filter whistles on its own.
context.osc3.freq: In this sound: how long each sweep takes.
context.osc3.tri: In this sound: how far the filter sweeps, and so how many harmonics you hear.
context.osc1.freq: In this sound: the drone. Lower notes have harmonics closer together, so the scale has more steps.

tweaks.hear: The sweep goes up and down smoothly instead of climbing and dropping.
A deeper drone with more harmonics in each sweep.

sounds.name: Stereo Swing
sounds.ref: From the EMS manual — the output amplifiers
sounds.blurb: One oscillator on both channels, with two slow oscillators opening and closing each side in turn.
sounds.how: The manual’s output amplifier example: B1 B2 C1 C2 O4 P6. Oscillator 1 goes to both channels. Oscillator 2 and Oscillator 3, both slow and slightly out of step, move the two channels’ levels through columns O and P, so the sound swings between left and right. Here the keyboard is also pinned to Oscillator 1 (I8) so you can play it.

steps.title: Oscillator 1 on both sides, from the keys
steps.why:
Sine and ramp mixed by pinning both rows to both outputs, and the keyboard on Oscillator 1.
- Pins B1, B2, C1, C2 and I8.
- Oscillator 1 sine LEVEL 6, ramp LEVEL 3: mostly sine, a little edge.
- INPUT LEVEL CHANNEL 1 at 5.
- Listen for: a plain tone in both speakers, following the keys.

steps.title: Two slow oscillators on the levels
steps.why:
Oscillator 2’s triangle moves channel 1’s level (O4) and Oscillator 3’s triangle moves channel 2’s (P6). They run at slightly different speeds, so the swing keeps changing.
- Pins O4 and P6.
- Oscillator 2 FREQUENCY 1.5 (2.4 Hz), triangle LEVEL 7.
- Oscillator 3 FREQUENCY 5.3 (3.4 Hz), triangle LEVEL 7.
- OUTPUT LEVEL 6.5 on both: the middle of the swing, so each channel opens and closes.
- Listen for: the tone throbbing and moving from side to side.

context.out1.level: In this sound: the centre of channel 1’s swing. Higher and it never fully closes; lower and it is silent half the time.
context.osc2.freq: In this sound: the speed of channel 1’s throb.
context.osc3.freq: In this sound: the speed of channel 2’s throb, a little faster than channel 1.
context.osc1.ramp: In this sound: adds brightness to the sine.

tweaks.hear: The two sides now throb at nearly the same speed, so the pattern repeats slowly.
The right side cuts out for half of each throb: a chopping effect.

sounds.name: Ring-Modulated Clangs
sounds.ref: From the EMS manual — the reverberation unit
sounds.blurb: Two oscillators ring-modulated, chopped by the repeating envelope and thrown into the spring reverb.
sounds.how: The manual’s reverb example: E2 F4 D13 G12 B14 I15 J16 (the manual prints the envelope pin as B13; it has to be D13). The ring modulator gives a metallic clang, the envelope shaper strikes it over and over, and the spring reverb catches every strike. The joystick retunes the two oscillators, which changes the clang completely. Row 14 also goes to channel 2 here, so it plays on both sides.

steps.title: Ramp times triangle
steps.why:
Oscillator 1’s ramp into ring modulator input A, Oscillator 2’s triangle into input B.
- Pins E2 and F4.
- Oscillator 1 FREQUENCY 6.3 (370 Hz), ramp LEVEL 6.
- Oscillator 2 FREQUENCY 6.75 (560 Hz), triangle LEVEL 6.
- Ring modulator LEVEL 7.
- Nothing is heard yet: row 13 is not pinned to an output.

steps.title: Strike it with the envelope
steps.why:
The ring modulator goes into the envelope shaper (D13). The envelope repeats on its own, so the clang is struck again and again.
- Pin D13.
- ATTACK 0, ON 0, DECAY 5 (0.2 s), OFF 2.5 (0.13 s): short strikes, about three a second.
- SIGNAL LEVEL 8.
- Still not heard: the shaped signal goes to the reverb next.

steps.title: Through the spring reverb
steps.why:
The shaped signal (row 12) into the reverb (G12), and the reverb (row 14) to both outputs.
- Pins G12, B14 and C14.
- Reverb MIX 5, LEVEL 9.
- Listen for: metallic strikes ringing on into a twangy spring echo.

steps.title: The joystick changes the clang
steps.why:
The joystick’s horizontal moves Oscillator 1 (I15), its vertical Oscillator 2 (J16).
- Pins I15 and J16.
- RANGE 3 on both.
- Try: move the stick while it plays. Each position gives a different metal.

context.env.decay: In this sound: the length of each strike. Longer strikes blur together in the reverb.
context.env.off: In this sound: the gap between strikes.
context.rev.mix: In this sound: how much spring is in the result. Towards 10 the strikes turn into a wash.
context.osc2.freq: In this sound: the ratio to Oscillator 1 decides the metal. Simple ratios sound more musical; odd ones clang.

tweaks.hear: The clang slides through different metallic tones.

tweaks.try: Turn OFF to 10 and play keys
tweaks.hear: One strike per key, each left ringing in the spring.

sounds.name: Filter Whistle Lead
sounds.ref: Classic technique: the filter played as a sine oscillator
sounds.blurb: The purest tone in the VCS3: the filter whistling on its own, played from the keys.
sounds.how: With RESPONSE past 6 the filter makes its own sine wave, cleaner than any of the oscillators. Pinning the keyboard voltage (row 8) into the filter frequency column N plays it, and the envelope shaper gives each note a soft start and end. The filter is more sensitive than the oscillators, so INPUT LEVEL CHANNEL 1 is turned down to about 3 to keep it in tune.

steps.title: Make the filter whistle
steps.why:
Nothing goes into the filter: RESPONSE 8 makes it oscillate on its own.
- Filter FREQUENCY 5.2 (about middle C), RESPONSE 8, LEVEL 5.
- Not heard yet: the filter’s row is not pinned.

steps.title: Shape it and send it out
steps.why:
The filter (row 10) into the envelope shaper (D10), and the shaped signal to both outputs.
- Pins D10, B12 and C12.
- ATTACK 2.5, ON 0, DECAY 5.5, OFF 10: a soft start, a gentle fade after each key, and no repeats.
- SIGNAL LEVEL 7.
- Listen for: a pure, flute-like tone when you press a key, all at one pitch.

steps.title: Play it from the keys
steps.why:
The keyboard voltage (row 8) into the filter frequency (N8).
- Pin N8.
- INPUT LEVEL CHANNEL 1 at 3.1: the filter moves an octave for every 0.2 V, more than the oscillators, so it needs less voltage to stay in tune.
- Listen for: a clean melody. If it drifts out of tune going up, nudge INPUT LEVEL CHANNEL 1.

context.vcf.response: In this sound: past 6.6 the filter oscillates. Below about 6 it stops, and with nothing pinned into it there is silence.
context.in.ch1: In this sound: the tuning of the keyboard for the filter. 3.1 is about one semitone per key.
context.vcf.freq: In this sound: where the keyboard starts. Turn it to transpose.
context.env.attack: In this sound: the soft start of each note.

tweaks.hear: The tone gets weaker: the filter is only just oscillating.
Quarter-tone steps: every key is half a semitone apart.

sounds.name: Machine Throb
sounds.ref: In the style of Pink Floyd — "Welcome to the Machine"
sounds.blurb: A low, filtered drone that pulses on and off through the output amplifiers.
sounds.how: Two low oscillators, almost in tune, go through the filter and the reverb. Oscillator 3’s square, at a little under twice a second, moves both output levels, so the drone throbs like a machine. The keyboard is pinned to both oscillators so you can move the drone around.

steps.title: Two low oscillators through the filter
steps.why:
Oscillator 1’s ramp and Oscillator 2’s square into the filter, both following the keys.
- Pins H2, H3, I8 and J8.
- Oscillator 1 FREQUENCY 6, ramp LEVEL 6; Oscillator 2 FREQUENCY 6.02, square LEVEL 5: almost in tune, so they beat slowly. With the keyboard pinned, the dial sets the pitch of middle C; the riff plays low E, about 82 Hz.
- INPUT LEVEL CHANNEL 1 at 5.
- Filter FREQUENCY 5 (220 Hz), RESPONSE 5, LEVEL 7: dark, with a ringing edge.

steps.title: Into the reverb and out
steps.why:
The filter into the reverb (G10), and the reverb to both outputs (B14, C14).
- Reverb MIX 4, LEVEL 8: mostly dry, with a spring tail.
- Listen for: a dark, steady drone.

steps.title: Oscillator 3 throbs the outputs
steps.why:
Oscillator 3’s square into both output level columns (O5, P5). The amplifiers open and shut with it.
- Oscillator 3 FREQUENCY 4.5 (1.6 Hz), square LEVEL 6.
- OUTPUT LEVEL 6.5 on both: set so the square nearly shuts the channels on its low half.
- Listen for: the drone pulsing, with the reverb filling the gaps.

context.osc3.freq: In this sound: the speed of the throb.
context.out1.level: In this sound: lower and the gaps go silent; higher and the throb gets shallower.
context.vcf.freq: In this sound: how dark the drone is.
context.osc2.freq: In this sound: tuned a hair above Oscillator 1, so the two beat slowly.

tweaks.hear: Short pulses of sound with longer gaps between them.
A whistling ring on top of the drone.

sounds.name: Pulsing Organ Filter
sounds.ref: In the style of The Who — "Won’t Get Fooled Again"
sounds.blurb: An organ-like tone whose filter opens and shuts in fast, even pulses.
sounds.how: On the record an organ was fed into a VCS3 and its filter pulsed by the envelope shaper. There is no outside input here, so two oscillators an octave apart stand in for the organ. The repeating trapezoid is pinned to the filter frequency (N11): it goes negative while the envelope is up, and a falling voltage raises the filter, so every cycle is a quick bright burst.

steps.title: An organ from two oscillators
steps.why:
Oscillator 1’s sine an octave above Oscillator 2’s square, both into the filter and both following the keys.
- Pins H1, H3, I8 and J8.
- Oscillator 1 FREQUENCY 6.67 (an octave above middle C), sine LEVEL 5.
- Oscillator 2 FREQUENCY 6, square LEVEL 5.
- INPUT LEVEL CHANNEL 1 at 5.

steps.title: A dark filter to both outputs
steps.why:
The filter (row 10) to both outputs.
- Pins B10 and C10.
- Filter FREQUENCY 5.5 (330 Hz), RESPONSE 4.5, LEVEL 8: muffled, with a little ring.
- Listen for: a dull organ tone.

steps.title: The trapezoid pulses the filter
steps.why:
The envelope’s own voltage, row 11, into the filter frequency (N11). The envelope repeats on its own about five times a second.
- Pin N11.
- TRAPEZOID LEVEL 4: the knob marked 11. Turning it up both deepens the pulse and closes the filter further between pulses.
- ATTACK 0, ON 1, DECAY 4, OFF 2: a fast rise, a short hold, a quick fall and a short rest.
- Listen for: the organ chopped into even, bright pulses.

context.env.off: In this sound: the gap between pulses, and so their speed.
context.env.trapLevel: In this sound: how far each pulse opens the filter.
context.vcf.freq: In this sound: where the pulses start from. Higher gives brighter, shallower pulses.
context.vcf.response: In this sound: a little ring on each pulse. Higher gives a squelch.

tweaks.hear: Each pulse fades more slowly, so they run into each other.
Each pulse squelches and whistles.

sounds.name: Space Swoops
sounds.ref: In the style of Hawkwind — "Silver Machine"
sounds.blurb: Two oscillators swooping up and down together, filtered and drenched in spring reverb.
sounds.how: Oscillator 3’s slow triangle is pinned to both audio oscillators’ frequency columns (I6, J6), so they glide up and down over more than an octave every few seconds. The filter takes the edge off and the reverb smears the swoops into a space-rock whoosh.

steps.title: Two oscillators through the filter
steps.why:
Oscillator 1’s ramp and Oscillator 2’s square into the filter.
- Pins H2 and H3.
- Oscillator 1 FREQUENCY 5.5 (156 Hz), ramp LEVEL 6; Oscillator 2 FREQUENCY 5.52, square LEVEL 5.
- Filter FREQUENCY 6.5 (700 Hz), RESPONSE 3, LEVEL 8.

steps.title: Into the reverb
steps.why:
The filter into the reverb (G10), and the reverb to both outputs.
- Pins G10, B14 and C14.
- Reverb MIX 6, LEVEL 8: more spring than dry.
- Listen for: a buzzing drone in a metallic space.

steps.title: Oscillator 3 makes it swoop
steps.why:
Oscillator 3’s triangle into both oscillators’ frequency columns, so they move together.
- Pins I6 and J6.
- Oscillator 3 FREQUENCY 3 (0.35 Hz, about three seconds a cycle), triangle LEVEL 6: more than an octave each way.
- Listen for: the drone swooping up and down like a passing spaceship.

context.osc3.tri: In this sound: how far the swoops go.
context.osc3.freq: In this sound: how fast the swoops are.
context.rev.mix: In this sound: how much the swoops are smeared.
context.vcf.freq: In this sound: how bright the swoops are.

tweaks.hear: A fast warble instead of a slow swoop.
A slow fall then a sudden jump back: a falling siren.

sounds.name: Chattering Treatment
sounds.ref: In the style of Roxy Music — "Ladytron"
sounds.blurb: Three oscillators modulating each other in a ring, so the pitch chatters and never quite repeats.
sounds.how: Oscillator 2 wobbles Oscillator 1 (I4), Oscillator 3 wobbles Oscillator 2 (J6), and Oscillator 1, at audio rate, shakes Oscillator 3 (K1). Each depends on the next, so the pattern drifts instead of looping, the kind of circular modulation the manual suggests for pseudo-random patterns. The reverb places it in a room.

steps.title: Oscillator 1 into the reverb
steps.why:
Oscillator 1’s sine into the reverb, and the reverb to both outputs.
- Pins G1, B14 and C14.
- Oscillator 1 FREQUENCY 6.5 (440 Hz), sine LEVEL 6.
- Reverb MIX 5, LEVEL 8.
- Listen for: a plain whistle in a spring room.

steps.title: Oscillator 2 wobbles it
steps.why:
Oscillator 2’s triangle into Oscillator 1’s frequency (I4).
- Oscillator 2 FREQUENCY 2.5 (7 Hz), triangle LEVEL 4: a wide, fast warble.
- Listen for: a bird-like trill.

steps.title: Close the loop
steps.why:
Oscillator 3 changes Oscillator 2’s speed (J6), and Oscillator 1 shakes Oscillator 3 (K1).
- Pins J6 and K1.
- Oscillator 3 FREQUENCY 4 (1 Hz), triangle LEVEL 5.
- Listen for: the trill speeding up and slowing down, chattering and squiggling in a pattern that keeps changing.

context.osc2.tri: In this sound: how wide the warble on Oscillator 1 is.
context.osc3.tri: In this sound: how much the warble speeds up and slows down.
context.osc1.sine: In this sound: also how hard Oscillator 1 shakes Oscillator 3, because the row goes to both the reverb and column K.
context.osc2.freq: In this sound: the basic speed of the warble.

tweaks.hear: Wild leaps of pitch instead of a trill.
The chatter slows into long, lazy curves.

sounds.name: Running Sequence
sounds.ref: In the style of Pink Floyd — "On the Run"
sounds.blurb: A fast, filtered pulse line where every note is a short, bright blip.
sounds.how: On the record the line came from the sequencer of a Synthi AKS, the VCS3’s briefcase sibling. Here the keyboard plays it: Oscillator 2’s pulse goes through the filter, and the trapezoid (N11) opens the filter for each note while the envelope shaper cuts it short.

steps.title: A pulse wave from the keys
steps.why:
Oscillator 2’s square into the filter, following the keyboard.
- Pins H3 and J8.
- Oscillator 2 FREQUENCY 6 (middle C on the keys), square LEVEL 6, SHAPE 3: a narrower pulse, more nasal than a square.
- INPUT LEVEL CHANNEL 1 at 5.

steps.title: Short notes through the envelope
steps.why:
The filter into the envelope shaper (D10) and on to both outputs (B12, C12). The envelope waits for each key.
- Filter FREQUENCY 5.5 (330 Hz), RESPONSE 5.5, LEVEL 8.
- ATTACK 0, ON 0, DECAY 3.5 (60 ms), OFF 10.
- SIGNAL LEVEL 8.
- Listen for: short, dark blips.

steps.title: The trapezoid opens the filter
steps.why:
The trapezoid into the filter frequency (N11), so each note starts bright and closes as the envelope falls.
- Pin N11.
- TRAPEZOID LEVEL 3.5.
- Listen for: each blip snapping open, the classic sequencer sound.

context.env.decay: In this sound: the length of each blip.
context.env.trapLevel: In this sound: how bright each note gets.
context.vcf.response: In this sound: the squelch on each note.
context.osc2.shape: In this sound: the width of the pulse. 5 is a hollow square; further from 5 is thinner.

tweaks.hear: Each note pings and whistles as the filter opens.
Longer notes that run into each other.

sounds.name: Wind and Waves
sounds.ref: In the style of Jean-Michel Jarre — Oxygène
sounds.blurb: Noise through a whistling filter that rises and falls, deep in the spring reverb.
sounds.how: Noise into a filter turned up until it nearly oscillates, so it howls at its frequency. Oscillator 3 slowly sweeps that frequency up and down, which is the rise and fall of the wind, and the reverb gives it distance. The joystick’s vertical axis is also pinned to the filter, so you can push the gusts higher by hand.

steps.title: Noise through a howling filter
steps.why:
Noise into the filter.
- Pin H7.
- Noise LEVEL 8, COLOUR 4: slightly dark.
- Filter FREQUENCY 6.5 (700 Hz), RESPONSE 6.3: just short of whistling on its own, so the noise howls.
- Filter LEVEL 7.

steps.title: Into the reverb and out
steps.why:
The filter into the reverb, and the reverb to both outputs.
- Pins G10, B14 and C14.
- Reverb MIX 6, LEVEL 9.
- Listen for: a steady wind in a large space.

steps.title: Gusts from Oscillator 3
steps.why:
Oscillator 3 sweeps the filter (N6), and the joystick can push it further (N16).
- Pins N6 and N16.
- Oscillator 3 FREQUENCY 3 (0.35 Hz), triangle LEVEL 5.
- Vertical RANGE 5.
- Listen for: the wind rising and falling every few seconds. Pull the stick down for higher gusts.

context.vcf.response: In this sound: how much the wind howls. Too high and the filter whistles on its own.
context.osc3.freq: In this sound: the speed of the gusts.
context.noise.colour: In this sound: darker is a rumble, lighter is a hiss.
context.rev.mix: In this sound: how far away the wind sounds.

tweaks.try: Pull the joystick down and let it back slowly
tweaks.hear: You push the wind higher and let it fall by hand.
Soft surf instead of a howl.

sounds.name: Staircase Pattern
sounds.ref: Classic technique: summed square waves on one oscillator
sounds.blurb: Two square waves at different speeds add up to a repeating four-note pattern, chopped by the envelope.
sounds.how: Pins in one column add together. Oscillator 2’s square (I3) jumps Oscillator 1 by a fifth, and Oscillator 3’s slower square (I5) jumps it by an octave, so between them the pitch steps round four notes. The levels of the two squares set the intervals. The repeating envelope chops it into blips, and the keyboard (I8) moves the whole pattern.

steps.title: Blips from the envelope
steps.why:
Oscillator 1’s sine through the repeating envelope to both outputs, following the keys.
- Pins D1, B12, C12 and I8.
- Oscillator 1 FREQUENCY 6, sine LEVEL 6.
- ATTACK 0, ON 0, DECAY 3, OFF 1.5: a quick blip, about ten a second.
- SIGNAL LEVEL 8. INPUT LEVEL CHANNEL 1 at 5.
- Listen for: a fast stream of blips at one pitch.

steps.title: A fifth from Oscillator 2
steps.why:
Oscillator 2’s square into Oscillator 1’s frequency (I3).
- Oscillator 2 FREQUENCY 2 (4.4 Hz), square LEVEL 2.4: just enough voltage to jump a fifth.
- Listen for: the blips trilling between two notes a fifth apart.

steps.title: An octave from Oscillator 3
steps.why:
Oscillator 3’s square, slower, into the same column (I5). It adds to Oscillator 2’s jump.
- Oscillator 3 FREQUENCY 4.5 (1.6 Hz), square LEVEL 3.2: an octave.
- Listen for: the trill jumping up and down an octave, a four-note pattern.

context.osc2.square: In this sound: the size of the small jump. 2.4 is about a fifth.
context.osc3.square: In this sound: the size of the big jump. 3.2 is about an octave.
context.osc2.freq: In this sound: the speed of the small jump.
context.osc3.freq: In this sound: the speed of the big jump.

tweaks.hear: The small jump shrinks to about a fourth.
The upper octave lasts longer than the lower one, so the pattern turns lopsided.

sounds.name: Growling FM Bass
sounds.ref: Classic technique: one oscillator shaking another’s pitch
sounds.blurb: A low oscillator whose pitch is shaken at audio rate by another, giving a metallic growl.
sounds.how: Oscillator 2’s triangle, at the same pitch as Oscillator 1, goes into Oscillator 1’s frequency column (I4). At audio rate that is frequency modulation: you hear new overtones rather than a wobble. Both oscillators follow the keys, so the growl stays the same on every note. The envelope shaper turns it into separate notes.

steps.title: A bass note through the envelope
steps.why:
Oscillator 1’s ramp through the envelope shaper to both outputs, following the keys.
- Pins D2, B12, C12 and I8.
- Oscillator 1 FREQUENCY 6, ramp LEVEL 5: with the keyboard pinned the dial sets middle C, and the riff plays two octaves below it. INPUT LEVEL CHANNEL 1 at 5.
- ATTACK 0, ON 0, DECAY 4.5 (0.15 s), OFF 10: the note holds while the key is down, then stops quickly.
- SIGNAL LEVEL 7.

steps.title: Oscillator 2 shakes its pitch
steps.why:
Oscillator 2’s triangle into Oscillator 1’s frequency (I4), with Oscillator 2 also following the keys (J8).
- Oscillator 2 FREQUENCY 6, the same as Oscillator 1, triangle LEVEL 3.5.
- Listen for: a harder, metallic growl on every note. Turn the triangle LEVEL up for more.

context.osc2.tri: In this sound: how much growl. Higher gives more overtones.
context.osc2.freq: In this sound: the same as Oscillator 1, so the growl is harmonic. Move it and the tone turns clangy.
context.env.decay: In this sound: how quickly each note stops after you let go.
context.osc1.freq: In this sound: the tuning of the whole keyboard. Keep Oscillator 2 at the same setting for a harmonic growl.

tweaks.hear: An octave up: a brighter, more hollow growl.
A harsh, buzzing metallic tone.

sounds.name: Trapezoid Pluck
sounds.ref: Classic technique: the envelope’s own voltage sweeping the filter
sounds.blurb: A pulse bass whose filter snaps open on each key and closes as the note fades.
sounds.how: The trapezoid on row 11 is the envelope as a voltage. It goes negative while the envelope is up, and on the VCS3 a falling voltage raises the filter, so pinning it to column N opens the filter on each note. The same envelope also shapes the loudness through column D. Its resting voltage pushes the filter down, which is why the filter knob sits higher than you might expect.

steps.title: A pulse through the filter
steps.why:
Oscillator 2’s pulse into the filter, following the keys.
- Pins H3 and J8.
- Oscillator 2 FREQUENCY 6 (middle C on the keys; the riff plays an octave and more below), square LEVEL 7, SHAPE 2: a fairly narrow pulse.
- INPUT LEVEL CHANNEL 1 at 5.
- Filter FREQUENCY 6.5, RESPONSE 5, LEVEL 8.

steps.title: Shape the loudness
steps.why:
The filter through the envelope shaper to both outputs.
- Pins D10, B12 and C12.
- ATTACK 0, ON 0, DECAY 4.5, OFF 10: each key gives one short note.
- SIGNAL LEVEL 8.
- Listen for: short notes with a steady tone.

steps.title: The trapezoid sweeps the filter
steps.why:
The trapezoid into the filter frequency (N11).
- Pin N11.
- TRAPEZOID LEVEL 4.5: each note opens the filter by about two octaves; between notes it sits about two octaves lower than the knob says.
- Listen for: a pluck on every note, bright at the start and darkening as it fades.

context.env.trapLevel: In this sound: the depth of the pluck.
context.vcf.freq: In this sound: the centre of the sweep. The trapezoid moves it down at rest and up during each note.
context.vcf.response: In this sound: the squelch of the pluck.
context.env.decay: In this sound: how long the note and the sweep last.

tweaks.hear: A squelchy, acid-like pluck.
Longer notes with a slower, wah-like close.

sounds.name: Joystick Duet
sounds.ref: Classic technique: two oscillators bent by hand
sounds.blurb: Two oscillators, one on each side, each bent by one axis of the joystick.
sounds.how: Oscillator 1’s sine goes to the left output and Oscillator 2’s triangle to the right. The joystick’s horizontal is pinned to Oscillator 1 (I15) and its vertical to Oscillator 2 (J16), so one hand plays two pitches at once. The RANGE knobs set how far each axis bends.

steps.title: One oscillator on each side
steps.why:
Oscillator 1’s sine to channel 1 (left), Oscillator 2’s triangle to channel 2 (right).
- Pins B1 and C4.
- Oscillator 1 FREQUENCY 6, sine LEVEL 6. Oscillator 2 FREQUENCY 6.4, triangle LEVEL 6: about a fifth above.
- Listen for: two steady tones, one in each speaker.

steps.title: The joystick bends them
steps.why:
The joystick’s horizontal to Oscillator 1 (I15), its vertical to Oscillator 2 (J16).
- RANGE 3 on both: several semitones each way.
- Try: drag the stick. Left and right bend the left tone; up and down bend the right one. Up lowers the pitch, because the oscillators rise as their voltage falls.

context.joy.rangeX: In this sound: how far the stick bends the left tone.
context.joy.rangeY: In this sound: how far the stick bends the right tone.
context.osc2.freq: In this sound: the interval between the two tones with the stick in the middle.

tweaks.try: Move the stick in a slow circle
tweaks.hear: The two tones weave round each other.
Several octaves of bend: a swooping siren.

sounds.name: Ring-Mod Bell Melody
sounds.ref: Classic technique: two oscillators that track the keys, ring-modulated
sounds.blurb: A bell tone you can play in tune: two oscillators both follow the keys, so their ring-modulated overtones move with the melody.
sounds.how: A ring modulator gives only the sum and difference of its two inputs. If both oscillators follow the keyboard (I8 and J8), the ratio between them stays the same on every key, so the bell keeps its character up and down the keyboard. Oscillator 2 sits 3.5 times above Oscillator 1, which puts the sum and difference on the 5th and 9th harmonics of the note you play. The envelope shaper strikes each note and the spring reverb holds the tail on the right.

steps.title: Two oscillators into the ring modulator
steps.why:
Oscillator 1’s sine into input A, Oscillator 2’s triangle into input B.
- Pins E1 and F4.
- Oscillator 1 FREQUENCY 6.67, sine LEVEL 6.
- Oscillator 2 FREQUENCY 7.87, triangle LEVEL 6: 3.5 times higher than Oscillator 1.
- Ring modulator LEVEL 7.
- Listen for: nothing yet. Row 13 is not pinned to an output.

steps.title: Both oscillators follow the keys
steps.why:
The keyboard voltage (row 8) into both frequency columns, so the pair moves together and the ratio between them holds.
- Pins I8 and J8.
- INPUT LEVEL CHANNEL 1 at 5: one semitone per key on both oscillators.
- Listen for: still nothing. The ring modulator has not been sent anywhere.

steps.title: Strike each note
steps.why:
The ring modulator into the envelope shaper (D13), and the shaped signal to both outputs.
- Pins D13, B12 and C12.
- ATTACK 0, ON 0, DECAY 6.8 (about 1 s), OFF 10: one strike per key, ringing on after you let go.
- SIGNAL LEVEL 8.
- Listen for: a bell on every key, in tune with the melody.

steps.title: Spring reverb on the right
steps.why:
The shaped signal also feeds the reverb (G12), and the reverb joins channel 2 (C14), which is panned right.
- Pins G12 and C14.
- Reverb MIX 6, LEVEL 7.
- Listen for: the dry strike on the left and a spring tail on the right.

context.osc2.freq: In this sound: the ratio to Oscillator 1, which decides the bell. 7.87 is 3.5 times higher and stays in tune; other settings give clangier, out-of-tune bells.
context.in.ch1: In this sound: the keyboard’s reach on both oscillators. Away from 5 the two still move together, but the melody comes out squeezed or stretched.
context.env.decay: In this sound: how long each bell rings.
context.ring.level: In this sound: the volume of the bell before the envelope shaper.
context.rev.mix: In this sound: how much spring is on the right-hand side.

tweaks.hear: The ratio is no longer simple, so the bell turns into a clanging, out-of-tune gong that still follows the melody.
The sine gains harmonics, so more overtones come out of the ring modulator: a harsher, more metallic bell.

sounds.name: Flying Saucer
sounds.ref: In the style of 1970s BBC Radiophonic Workshop sci-fi effects
sounds.blurb: The filter’s own sine tone, warbling fast, rising and sinking on a slow repeating envelope.
sounds.how: The filter makes the tone itself, with RESPONSE past 6 and nothing pinned into it. Oscillator 3, running at about seven cycles a second, shakes its frequency (N6) for the warble. The trapezoid is pinned to the same column (N11), so each slow cycle of the envelope lifts the pitch and lets it sink back as the sound fades. The envelope repeats on its own, so the craft comes and goes with no key held.

steps.title: The filter as a sine oscillator
steps.why:
Nothing goes into the filter: with RESPONSE 8 it whistles by itself.
- Filter FREQUENCY 6.5 (700 Hz), RESPONSE 8, LEVEL 5.
- Listen for: nothing yet. Row 10 is not pinned anywhere.

steps.title: A slow repeating envelope
steps.why:
The filter into the envelope shaper (D10), then through the reverb (G12) to both outputs (B14 and C14).
- Pins D10, G12, B14 and C14.
- ATTACK 8 (0.3 s), ON 6 (0.9 s), DECAY 8 (2.7 s), OFF 5 (1.8 s): a slow rise, a hold, a long fade and a rest, round and round.
- SIGNAL LEVEL 8. Reverb MIX 5, LEVEL 8.
- Listen for: a pure tone fading in and out every few seconds, at one pitch.

steps.title: Oscillator 3 makes it warble
steps.why:
Oscillator 3’s triangle into the filter frequency (N6). At this speed it is a wide, fast vibrato.
- Pin N6.
- Oscillator 3 FREQUENCY 5.9 (7 Hz), triangle LEVEL 4: almost an octave each way.
- Listen for: the tone wobbling up and down several times a second.

steps.title: The trapezoid lifts and drops it
steps.why:
The envelope’s own voltage (row 11) into the filter frequency too (N11). It falls while the envelope is up, and a falling voltage raises the filter, so the pitch climbs with each rise and sinks with each fade.
- Pin N11.
- TRAPEZOID LEVEL 3: about an octave each way.
- Listen for: the warbling tone swooping up as it arrives and sinking away as it goes.

context.vcf.response: In this sound: past 6.6 the filter makes the tone. Below that there is silence, because nothing is pinned into the filter.
context.osc3.freq: In this sound: the speed of the warble.
context.osc3.tri: In this sound: the width of the warble.
context.env.trapLevel: In this sound: how far each arrival lifts the pitch.
context.env.off: In this sound: the gap between arrivals. Past 6 the envelope waits for a key or the ATTACK button.

tweaks.hear: A slow, lazy wobble instead of a fast warble.

tweaks.try: Turn OFF to 10, then click the ATTACK button on and off
tweaks.hear: One arrival each time you press it: you fire the effect by hand.
The warble becomes a ramp, so the pitch keeps climbing and snapping back: a busier, more mechanical sound.

sounds.name: Joystick Dive
sounds.ref: Classic technique: pitch and filter played on one stick
sounds.blurb: A buzzing two-oscillator drone you dive and climb with the joystick, one axis for pitch and the other for brightness.
sounds.how: The joystick gives two voltages at once. Here the vertical axis (row 16) goes to both oscillators’ frequency columns (I16, J16), so pushing the stick up dives the pitch and pulling it down climbs. The horizontal axis (row 15) goes to the filter frequency (N15), so the same hand opens and closes the tone. The spring reverb catches the end of each move.

steps.title: Two oscillators through the filter
steps.why:
Oscillator 1’s ramp and Oscillator 2’s square into the filter, nearly in tune so they beat.
- Pins H2 and H3.
- Oscillator 1 FREQUENCY 6, ramp LEVEL 6; Oscillator 2 FREQUENCY 6.03, square LEVEL 5.
- Filter FREQUENCY 7 (1 kHz), RESPONSE 4, LEVEL 8.
- Listen for: nothing yet. Row 10 goes out in the next step.

steps.title: Through the reverb to both sides
steps.why:
The filter into the reverb (G10), and the reverb to both outputs.
- Pins G10, B14 and C14.
- Reverb MIX 3, LEVEL 8: mostly dry, with a spring tail.
- Listen for: a steady, slightly beating buzz.

steps.title: Up and down: the pitch
steps.why:
The joystick’s vertical (row 16) into both oscillators’ frequency columns, so they move together and keep beating at the same rate.
- Pins I16 and J16.
- Vertical RANGE 6: up to about three octaves each way.
- Push the stick slowly up for a long dive, then pull it down past the middle to climb.
- Listen for: the whole drone sliding down and up with the stick.

steps.title: Left and right: the brightness
steps.why:
The joystick’s horizontal (row 15) into the filter frequency (N15).
- Pin N15.
- Horizontal RANGE 3.
- Move the stick right to close the filter and left to open it, while you dive.
- Listen for: the dive darkening as you lean right, so it sounds further away as it falls.

context.joy.rangeY: In this sound: how far the dive goes. At 10 the stick covers the whole audible range.
context.joy.rangeX: In this sound: how much the stick changes the brightness.
context.osc2.freq: In this sound: a hair above Oscillator 1, so the two beat. Both follow the stick, so the beat stays as you dive.
context.vcf.freq: In this sound: the brightness with the stick in the middle.

tweaks.try: Push the stick all the way up over two seconds, then let it spring back to the middle
tweaks.hear: A falling dive that ends in a low growl, then jumps back up to the drone.

tweaks.try: Move the stick in small fast circles
tweaks.hear: The pitch and the brightness wobble together, a hand-made vibrato and wah.
A ringing peak that whistles as you sweep left and right.

sounds.name: Self-Playing Rhythm
sounds.ref: Classic technique: a repeating envelope and free-running oscillators
sounds.blurb: A rhythm of filtered noise and low thuds that plays itself, with no keys, and keeps shifting.
sounds.how: With OFF below 6 the envelope shaper repeats on its own, so it is the clock. Its trapezoid opens the filter on each hit (N11). Oscillator 3, running at its own speed, switches the filter between bright and dull hits with its square (N5) and stretches and shortens each decay with its triangle (L6), which also moves the timing. The envelope and Oscillator 3 are not locked together, so the pattern slowly changes as they drift in and out of step.

steps.title: Noise and a low square into the filter
steps.why:
Noise and Oscillator 2’s square both into the filter.
- Pins H7 and H3.
- Noise LEVEL 6, COLOUR 6: a little brighter than white.
- Oscillator 2 FREQUENCY 4.86 (80 Hz), square LEVEL 5: the thud.
- Filter FREQUENCY 6 (480 Hz), RESPONSE 4, LEVEL 9.
- Listen for: nothing yet. Row 10 goes to the envelope shaper next.

steps.title: The envelope is the clock
steps.why:
The filter into the envelope shaper (D10) and the shaped signal to both outputs.
- Pins D10, B12 and C12.
- ATTACK 0, ON 0, DECAY 4.5 (0.14 s), OFF 2.2 (0.1 s): a short hit about four times a second.
- SIGNAL LEVEL 8.
- Listen for: an even run of dull hits, with no key pressed.

steps.title: The trapezoid opens the filter
steps.why:
The envelope’s own voltage into the filter frequency (N11): each hit starts bright and closes as it decays.
- Pin N11.
- TRAPEZOID LEVEL 4.
- Listen for: crisp, snappy hits instead of dull ones.

steps.title: Oscillator 3 makes the pattern
steps.why:
Oscillator 3’s square into the filter frequency (N5) and its triangle into the decay time (L6).
- Pins N5 and L6.
- Oscillator 3 FREQUENCY 4.45 (1.6 Hz), square LEVEL 4, triangle LEVEL 6.
- The square gives alternate groups of bright, hissy hits and dark thuds; the triangle makes the hits longer and slower, then shorter and quicker.
- Listen for: a lopsided pattern of ticks and thuds that never settles into a straight loop.

context.env.off: In this sound: the rest between hits, and so the tempo. Past 6 it stops and waits for a key.
context.env.decay: In this sound: the length of each hit, before Oscillator 3 stretches it.
context.osc3.freq: In this sound: how fast the pattern changes between bright and dark hits.
context.osc3.tri: In this sound: how much the hit lengths, and so the timing, swing.
context.env.trapLevel: In this sound: how much each hit snaps the filter open.

tweaks.hear: The bright and dark groups get shorter, so the pattern turns busier.
A faster rhythm, nearly a roll.
Each hit pings at the filter frequency, like a tuned drum.

sounds.name: Spring Through the Filter
sounds.ref: Classic technique: the reverb in the middle of the patch
sounds.blurb: Short plucks thrown into the spring reverb, with the whole reverb then played through a ringing filter that Oscillator 3 sweeps.
sounds.how: On most synths the reverb is the last thing in the chain. On the VCS3 it is just another row and column, so its output can go anywhere, here into the filter (H14). With RESPONSE near the peak the filter rings at its own pitch every time the springs rattle, so each pluck leaves a whistling, pitched tail rather than a plain echo. Oscillator 3 moves the filter (N6), so the tails slide up and down.

steps.title: A pluck from the keys
steps.why:
Oscillator 2’s triangle through the envelope shaper, following the keys.
- Pins D4 and J8.
- Oscillator 2 FREQUENCY 6, triangle LEVEL 7. INPUT LEVEL CHANNEL 1 at 5.
- ATTACK 0, ON 0, DECAY 3.5 (60 ms), OFF 10: a short blip per key.
- SIGNAL LEVEL 7.
- Listen for: nothing yet. Row 12 goes to the reverb next.

steps.title: Into the springs, then the filter
steps.why:
The pluck into the reverb (G12), the reverb into the filter (H14), and the filter to both outputs (B10, C10). The filter starts wide open, so for now it changes little.
- Pins G12, H14, B10 and C10.
- Reverb MIX 8, LEVEL 7: mostly spring.
- Filter FREQUENCY 8 (2.2 kHz), RESPONSE 0, LEVEL 8.
- Listen for: short blips with a long, twangy spring tail.

steps.title: Make the filter ring
steps.why:
Bring the filter down and turn RESPONSE up until it nearly oscillates. Now every rattle of the springs sets it ringing at its own pitch.
- Filter FREQUENCY 6.5 (700 Hz), RESPONSE 6: right at the edge of oscillating.
- Listen for: the spring tail turning into a pitched whistle that rings on after each pluck.

steps.title: Oscillator 3 moves the whistle
steps.why:
Oscillator 3’s slow triangle into the filter frequency (N6), so the pitch of the ringing tail drifts.
- Pin N6.
- Oscillator 3 FREQUENCY 3 (0.35 Hz), triangle LEVEL 4.
- Listen for: the tails sliding up and down in pitch, each pluck landing on a different part of the sweep.

context.vcf.response: In this sound: how much the filter rings on the spring tail. Lower gives a plain reverb; a little higher and the filter whistles all the time.
context.rev.mix: In this sound: how much of the pluck reaches the filter as spring rather than dry. Towards 10 the plucks blur into the tails.
context.vcf.freq: In this sound: the centre pitch of the whistling tail.
context.osc3.tri: In this sound: how far the tails slide.
context.rev.level: In this sound: how hard the reverb drives the filter, so also how loud the result is.

tweaks.try: Sweep Filter FREQUENCY between 5.5 and 7.5 while the tails ring
tweaks.hear: You tune the ringing tail by hand.
The filter whistles all the time, and each pluck knocks the whistle about.

sounds.name: Breaking Waves
sounds.ref: Classic technique: noise, a slow envelope and the stereo outputs
sounds.blurb: Dark noise rising and falling in slow waves that break on the left and wash away on the right.
sounds.how: Noise goes through the filter and a slow, self-repeating envelope. The trapezoid opens the filter as each wave rises (N11), so it breaks brighter and sinks back to a rumble. The dry wave goes to channel 1, panned left, and the reverb to channel 2, panned right, so each wave lands on one side and its wash spreads to the other. Oscillator 3, very slow, stretches the decay (L6), so no two waves are the same length.

steps.title: Dark noise through the filter
steps.why:
Noise into the filter, and the filter into the envelope shaper.
- Pins H7 and D10.
- Noise LEVEL 8, COLOUR 3.5: darker than white, more rumble.
- Filter FREQUENCY 6 (480 Hz), RESPONSE 2, LEVEL 9.
- Listen for: nothing yet. The envelope shaper’s output is not pinned.

steps.title: Slow waves on the left
steps.why:
The shaped signal to channel 1 (B12), panned to the left.
- Pin B12.
- ATTACK 10 (1 s), ON 4 (0.4 s), DECAY 8.5 (4 s), OFF 4 (0.6 s): a slow surge, a short peak, a long draw-back and a pause.
- SIGNAL LEVEL 9.
- PAN CHANNEL 1 at 1.
- Listen for: a wave of noise building and falling away on the left, every five or six seconds.

steps.title: The trapezoid opens the filter
steps.why:
The envelope’s own voltage into the filter frequency (N11), so the noise brightens as each wave rises and darkens as it draws back.
- Pin N11.
- TRAPEZOID LEVEL 3.5.
- Listen for: a hiss at the top of each wave and a low rumble as it pulls away.

steps.title: The wash on the right
steps.why:
The shaped signal into the reverb (G12), and the reverb to channel 2 (C14), panned right.
- Pins G12 and C14.
- Reverb MIX 9, LEVEL 7: almost all spring.
- PAN CHANNEL 2 at 9.
- Listen for: each wave breaking on the left and its spray spreading to the right.

steps.title: Every wave a different length
steps.why:
Oscillator 3, very slow, into the decay time (L6).
- Pin L6.
- Oscillator 3 FREQUENCY 1.5 (one cycle every 14 s or so), triangle LEVEL 6.
- Listen for: some waves drawing back quickly, others lingering, so the timing never repeats exactly.

context.noise.colour: In this sound: below 5 for a heavier sea. Turn it up for a lighter, hissier surf.
context.env.attack: In this sound: how slowly each wave builds.
context.env.decay: In this sound: how long each wave takes to draw back.
context.env.trapLevel: In this sound: how much brighter the top of each wave is.
context.out2.pan: In this sound: where the reverb wash sits. Move it to the left and the sea closes in to one side.
context.osc3.tri: In this sound: how much the wave lengths vary.

tweaks.try: Turn OFF to 10 and click the ATTACK button on and off
tweaks.hear: One wave each time you press it.
The noise whistles at the top of each wave, more like wind than water.

sounds.name: Bubbling Cross-Modulation
sounds.ref: In the style of early-1970s space rock
sounds.blurb: A ringing filter pinged by one oscillator and retuned by another, while the two oscillators modulate each other.
sounds.how: Oscillator 2’s square, at eight cycles a second, goes into the filter (H3); with RESPONSE near the peak each edge makes the filter ring, a bloop. Oscillator 1’s sine moves the filter frequency (N1), so each bloop has a different pitch. Then the two oscillators are pinned into each other’s frequency columns (I3 and J1): each speeds up and slows down the other, so the pattern bubbles instead of repeating. This kind of loop is easy on a pin matrix and impossible on a fixed-path synth.

steps.title: A square pings the filter
steps.why:
Oscillator 2’s square into the filter, and the filter to both outputs.
- Pins H3, B10 and C10.
- Oscillator 2 FREQUENCY 2.65 (8 Hz), square LEVEL 6.
- Filter FREQUENCY 6 (480 Hz), RESPONSE 5.8, LEVEL 7: just short of oscillating, so each edge of the square rings.
- Listen for: an even run of ringing blips at one pitch.

steps.title: Oscillator 1 retunes each blip
steps.why:
Oscillator 1’s sine into the filter frequency (N1).
- Pin N1.
- Oscillator 1 FREQUENCY 2.25 (5.3 Hz), sine LEVEL 4: almost an octave each way.
- Listen for: the blips going up and down in pitch in a regular pattern.

steps.title: The oscillators modulate each other
steps.why:
Oscillator 2’s square into Oscillator 1’s frequency (I3) and Oscillator 1’s sine into Oscillator 2’s (J1). Each now changes the other’s speed.
- Pins I3 and J1.
- Listen for: the regular pattern breaking up into bubbling, uneven runs of blips.

steps.title: Into the spring
steps.why:
The filter also feeds the reverb (G10), and the reverb joins both outputs.
- Pins G10, B14 and C14.
- Reverb MIX 6, LEVEL 6.
- Listen for: the bubbles ringing on in the springs.

context.vcf.response: In this sound: how much each edge rings. Lower gives clicks; past 6.6 the filter whistles over everything.
context.osc2.freq: In this sound: the basic rate of the blips.
context.osc2.square: In this sound: how hard the blips ping the filter, and, through I3, how far Oscillator 2 throws Oscillator 1’s speed.
context.osc1.sine: In this sound: how far the blips move in pitch, and how much Oscillator 1 speeds and slows Oscillator 2.
context.osc1.freq: In this sound: how fast the pitch pattern moves.

tweaks.hear: Fast, boiling bubbles.
Oscillator 1 reaches audio rate: the blips turn rough and gritty.
Deeper, liquid bloops.

sounds.name: Left-to-Right Throws
sounds.ref: Classic technique: the trapezoid on an output amplifier
sounds.blurb: Plucked notes that land on the left and slide over to the right as they fade.
sounds.how: The same shaped signal goes to both outputs, one panned left and one right. The trapezoid, which goes negative while the envelope is up, is pinned to channel 2’s level (P11). So at the start of each note channel 2 is almost shut and the note is heard on the left; as the envelope falls, channel 2 opens and the tail moves across to the right. The envelope is moving the sound in space as well as in loudness.

steps.title: A pluck from the keys
steps.why:
Oscillator 1’s ramp and Oscillator 2’s square into the filter, both following the keys.
- Pins H2, H3, I8 and J8.
- Oscillator 1 FREQUENCY 6, ramp LEVEL 5; Oscillator 2 FREQUENCY 6.67 (an octave up), square LEVEL 4. INPUT LEVEL CHANNEL 1 at 5.
- Filter FREQUENCY 6.8, RESPONSE 3, LEVEL 8.
- Listen for: nothing yet. Row 10 goes to the envelope shaper next.

steps.title: One note, both sides
steps.why:
The filter through the envelope shaper (D10) to both outputs (B12, C12).
- ATTACK 0, ON 0, DECAY 7 (1.2 s), OFF 10: a strike and a long fade per key.
- SIGNAL LEVEL 8.
- OUTPUT LEVEL 1 at 7.5, OUTPUT LEVEL 2 at 7.5. PAN CHANNEL 1 at 0 (left), PAN CHANNEL 2 at 10 (right).
- Listen for: plucked notes in the middle of the stereo picture.

steps.title: The trapezoid moves channel 2
steps.why:
The trapezoid (row 11) into channel 2’s level (P11). It swings negative at the strike, closing the right side, and climbs back as the note fades, opening it.
- Pin P11.
- TRAPEZOID LEVEL 6.
- OUTPUT LEVEL 2 at 7.5: with the trapezoid added it is nearly shut at the strike and fully open between notes.
- Listen for: each note striking on the left and its tail sliding across to the right.

context.env.trapLevel: In this sound: how far each note travels. At 0 the notes stay in the middle.
context.env.decay: In this sound: how long the slide across takes.
context.out2.level: In this sound: the starting point for channel 2. Lower and the right side stays quieter throughout.
context.out1.pan: In this sound: where each note lands. Bring it to 5 and notes start in the middle before moving right.

tweaks.hear: The envelope repeats on its own, so the notes are thrown across again and again.
A slower glide across, nearly three seconds a note.

sounds.name: Singing Filter Drone
sounds.ref: Classic technique: an oscillating filter with something going through it
sounds.blurb: The filter whistling its own tone two octaves above a low ramp that runs through it, with the spring reverb breathing in and out.
sounds.how: With RESPONSE past 6 the filter is an oscillator, but it still passes what is pinned into it. Here a low ramp from Oscillator 1 goes through it (H2), so you hear the filtered ramp and the filter’s own sine over the top, two octaves higher, with the input pulling at the sine. Oscillator 2, at audio rate, shakes the filter frequency (N4) and roughens the sine. Oscillator 3 slowly moves the reverb MIX (M6), so the space around the drone grows and shrinks.

steps.title: The filter sings
steps.why:
No input yet: RESPONSE 7.5 makes the filter oscillate on its own, through the reverb to both outputs.
- Pins G10, B14 and C14.
- Filter FREQUENCY 5.2 (260 Hz, about middle C), RESPONSE 7.5, LEVEL 5.
- Reverb MIX 5, LEVEL 7.
- Listen for: a pure, steady sine.

steps.title: A low ramp through it
steps.why:
Oscillator 1’s ramp into the filter (H2), two octaves below the filter’s tone.
- Pin H2.
- Oscillator 1 FREQUENCY 4.67 (65 Hz), ramp LEVEL 5.
- Listen for: a dark buzz underneath, with the sine still singing on top and wavering slightly as the ramp pulls at it.

steps.title: Oscillator 2 roughens the sine
steps.why:
Oscillator 2’s triangle, at the same low pitch as Oscillator 1, into the filter frequency (N4). At audio rate that adds overtones rather than a wobble.
- Pin N4.
- Oscillator 2 FREQUENCY 4.67, triangle LEVEL 3.
- Listen for: the sine gaining a hoarse, vocal edge.

steps.title: Oscillator 3 breathes the reverb
steps.why:
Oscillator 3’s slow triangle into the reverb MIX (M6).
- Pin M6.
- Oscillator 3 FREQUENCY 2.5 (one cycle every five seconds), triangle LEVEL 9.
- Listen for: the drone moving closer and further away as the spring comes and goes.

context.vcf.response: In this sound: past 6.6 the filter sings its own tone. Below that you hear only the filtered ramp.
context.vcf.freq: In this sound: the pitch of the sung tone. Keep it a whole number of octaves above Oscillator 1 for a steady drone.
context.osc2.tri: In this sound: how rough the sine is. At 0 it is pure again.
context.osc1.ramp: In this sound: how loud the low buzz is, and how hard it pulls at the filter’s tone.
context.osc3.tri: In this sound: how far the reverb MIX swings.

tweaks.try: Move Filter FREQUENCY slowly between 5 and 5.4
tweaks.hear: The sung tone beats against the ramp’s harmonics, then locks in where they line up.
Out of step with the drone, the roughness turns into a clanging, metallic edge.

sounds.name: Electronic Toms
sounds.ref: Classic technique: the trapezoid bending pitch
sounds.blurb: Pitched drums from a sine wave: the trapezoid bends each hit downwards as it fades, and the keys tune them.
sounds.how: Oscillator 1’s sine and a little noise go through the envelope shaper, struck by each key. The trapezoid is pinned to Oscillator 1’s frequency (I11): it is at its lowest while the envelope is up, and a falling voltage raises the pitch, so each hit starts high and drops as it decays, like a struck drum skin. The keyboard (I8) tunes the drums, so the riff is a tom fill.

steps.title: A sine struck by each key
steps.why:
Oscillator 1’s sine through the envelope shaper to both outputs, following the keys.
- Pins D1, B12, C12 and I8.
- Oscillator 1 FREQUENCY 5 (93 Hz on middle C), sine LEVEL 7. INPUT LEVEL CHANNEL 1 at 5.
- ATTACK 0, ON 0, DECAY 5.5 (0.3 s), OFF 10. Each key is a short tap: while a key is held the envelope stays at the top.
- SIGNAL LEVEL 8.
- Listen for: low, dull beeps at the pitch of each key.

steps.title: The trapezoid bends the pitch
steps.why:
The trapezoid (row 11) into Oscillator 1’s frequency (I11).
- Pin I11.
- TRAPEZOID LEVEL 3: about eight semitones above the dial at the strike, falling to eight below as the hit dies.
- Listen for: each beep turning into a tom, starting high and dropping.

steps.title: Noise for the stick
steps.why:
A little noise into the envelope shaper too (D7), so each hit has a rattle on top.
- Pin D7.
- Noise LEVEL 2.5, COLOUR 7: thin and hissy.
- Listen for: a crisper attack on each tom.

context.env.trapLevel: In this sound: how far each hit drops. Higher gives a laser-like zap; lower a plain thud.
context.env.decay: In this sound: the length of each drum, and of its drop.
context.osc1.freq: In this sound: the tuning of the whole kit.
context.noise.level: In this sound: how much rattle sits on each hit.

tweaks.hear: Each hit sweeps down over two octaves: a disco-style electronic drum zap.
The rattle takes over: more snare than tom.

sounds.name: Random Computer Babble
sounds.ref: Classic technique: filtered noise as a random voltage
sounds.blurb: Fast blips whose pitch lurches about at random, the film-computer sound, made without a sample and hold.
sounds.how: The VCS3 Mk 1 has no sample and hold. Noise through the filter turned almost to the bottom (H7), with RESPONSE near the peak, is the next best thing: only a narrow band of slow movement around 16 Hz gets through, a wobbling voltage whose size and timing change at random. Pinned to Oscillator 1’s frequency (I10), it gives each blip from the repeating envelope a different pitch and a different bend. The same voltage on the decay column (L10) makes the blips uneven in length and speed.

steps.title: Fast blips from the envelope
steps.why:
Oscillator 1’s sine through the repeating envelope to both outputs.
- Pins D1, B12 and C12.
- Oscillator 1 FREQUENCY 7 (740 Hz), sine LEVEL 6.
- ATTACK 0, ON 0, DECAY 3.5 (60 ms), OFF 1.8: about eight blips a second.
- SIGNAL LEVEL 8.
- Listen for: a stream of blips at one pitch.

steps.title: Noise filtered into a slow random voltage
steps.why:
Noise into the filter (H7) with FREQUENCY almost at the bottom, so only its slowest movements get through. RESPONSE near the peak makes the filter ring on that band, which makes the voltage much bigger. The filter’s output is now a control voltage, not a sound.
- Pin H7.
- Noise LEVEL 10, COLOUR 0: the darkest noise has the most low movement in it.
- Filter FREQUENCY 1.5 (16 Hz), RESPONSE 6, LEVEL 10.
- Listen for: no change yet. Row 10 is not pinned.

steps.title: The random voltage plays the pitch
steps.why:
The filtered noise (row 10) into Oscillator 1’s frequency (I10).
- Pin I10.
- Listen for: the blips jumping about to unrelated pitches, never repeating a phrase.

steps.title: And the timing
steps.why:
The same voltage into the decay time (L10), so the length of each blip, and the gap to the next, wander too.
- Pin L10.
- Listen for: blips speeding up, hesitating and clustering, as if something were thinking.

context.vcf.freq: In this sound: how fast the random voltage moves. Higher and the pitch jitters within each blip; lower and it moves more slowly.
context.vcf.response: In this sound: how big the random voltage is. Lower and the filter rings less, so the pitches stay closer together.
context.vcf.level: In this sound: how wide the random pitches range.
context.noise.colour: In this sound: at 0 the noise is darkest, which gives the filter the most to pass.
context.env.off: In this sound: the basic rate of the blips.

tweaks.hear: The pitch now jitters inside each blip: a burbling, chattering sound.
The pitches stay closer together, more like muttering than shouting.

sounds.name: Berlin Ostinato Bass
sounds.ref: In the style of Klaus Schulze — “Picture Music” (1975)
sounds.blurb: A running sixteenth-note bass in E minor that plucks on every note while the whole line slowly brightens and darkens.
sounds.how: Oscillator 1’s ramp and Oscillator 2’s square an octave below it go through the filter, both following the keys. Two voltages meet in the filter frequency column N: the trapezoid (N11) gives each note its pluck, and Oscillator 3’s slow triangle (N6) sweeps the whole line over several bars. Every column of the matrix sums what is pinned into it, which is how one filter gets a pluck and a sweep at once.

steps.title: Two oscillators an octave apart
steps.why:
Oscillator 1’s ramp and Oscillator 2’s square into the filter, both following the keyboard.
- Pins H2, H3, I8 and J8. Unpin D2.
- Oscillator 1 FREQUENCY 6 · 262 Hz, ramp LEVEL 6 · 0.7 V; Oscillator 2 FREQUENCY 5.3 · 131 Hz, an octave lower, square LEVEL 5 · 0.5 V, SHAPE 5: a square.
- INPUT LEVEL CHANNEL 1 at 5 · 1 semitone per key: both oscillators play in tune from the keys.
- Filter FREQUENCY 5.5 · 327 Hz, RESPONSE 4.5 · sharp peak, LEVEL 8 · 1.3 V.
- Listen for: nothing yet: row 10 goes to the envelope shaper next.

steps.title: Short notes from the envelope shaper
steps.why:
The filter through the envelope shaper to both outputs. With OFF past 6 the envelope waits for each key.
- Pins D10, B12 and C12.
- Envelope ATTACK 0 · 2 ms, ON 0 · 0 ms, DECAY 3.8 · 76 ms, Envelope OFF 10 · manual: waits for a key.
- Envelope SIGNAL LEVEL 7 · 1.2 V.
- Listen for: short, dull bass notes.

steps.title: The trapezoid plucks the filter
steps.why:
The trapezoid, the envelope as a voltage, into the filter frequency. It swings negative while the envelope is up, and a falling voltage raises the filter.
- Pin N11.
- TRAPEZOID LEVEL 4 · 0.5 V: each note opens the filter by about two octaves.
- Listen for: a pluck on every sixteenth.

steps.title: Oscillator 3 sweeps the line
steps.why:
Oscillator 3’s triangle into the same column N. It adds to the trapezoid, so the plucks ride on a slow sweep.
- Pin N6.
- Oscillator 3 FREQUENCY 2.5 · 0.20 Hz: one sweep every five seconds. triangle LEVEL 5 · 0.4 V.
- Listen for: the ostinato slowly opening up and closing again, as a Berlin-school sequence does when someone rides the filter.

context.osc3.freq: In this sound: how slowly the line brightens and darkens.
context.env.trapLevel: In this sound: the depth of the pluck on each note.
context.vcf.freq: In this sound: the centre the pluck and the sweep move around.
context.osc2.freq: In this sound: an octave below Oscillator 1, for weight.

tweaks.hear: Each pluck rings with a whistle.
A deeper sweep, from muffled to bright.
Longer notes that blur into each other.

sounds.name: Keys Set the Decay
sounds.ref: In the style of Franco Battiato — “Fetus” (1972)
sounds.blurb: A breathy pulse bass in 7/8 whose low notes ring on while the high ones stop short.
sounds.how: The keyboard voltage on row 8 goes to Oscillator 2 as usual, and also to column L, the envelope’s decay time. Lower keys give a higher voltage there, and a rising voltage lengthens DECAY, so the low notes of the riff hang over while the high ones are clipped: the line phrases itself. A little dark noise in the filter gives each note a breath.

steps.title: A narrow pulse and dark noise
steps.why:
Oscillator 2’s pulse and the noise into the filter, Oscillator 2 following the keys.
- Pins H3, H7 and J8. Unpin D2 and I8.
- Oscillator 2 FREQUENCY 6 · 262 Hz, square LEVEL 6 · 0.7 V, SHAPE 8: a narrow, reedy pulse.
- Noise LEVEL 3 · 0.1 V, Noise COLOUR 3: dark noise, a breath under each note.
- INPUT LEVEL CHANNEL 1 at 5 · 1 semitone per key.
- Filter FREQUENCY 5.8 · 411 Hz, RESPONSE 3 · low-pass, LEVEL 8 · 1.3 V.
- Oscillator 1 ramp LEVEL 0 · 0 V: the Default patch’s sawtooth is not used.

steps.title: Notes from the envelope shaper
steps.why:
The filter through the envelope shaper to both outputs.
- Pins D10, B12 and C12.
- Envelope ATTACK 0 · 2 ms, ON 0 · 0 ms, DECAY 4.5 · 140 ms, Envelope OFF 10 · manual: waits for a key.
- Envelope SIGNAL LEVEL 7 · 1.2 V.
- Listen for: every note the same short length.

steps.title: The keys stretch the decay
steps.why:
The keyboard voltage into the decay column as well (L8). Row 8 rises as the keys go down, and every 0.4 V doubles DECAY.
- Pin L8.
- Low A gives about three times the knob’s decay, the A an octave up less than twice.
- Listen for: the low notes ringing into the next beat and the high ones stopping short, so the 7/8 riff lilts.

context.in.ch1: In this sound: also how strongly the keys change the decay. It moves the pitch too, so leave it at 5.
context.env.decay: In this sound: the shortest note length; the keys add to it.
context.osc2.shape: In this sound: the narrow pulse that gives the bass its reed.
context.noise.colour: In this sound: the breath. Lower is a rumble, higher a hiss.

tweaks.hear: A tight, staccato line; the low notes still ring a little longer.
A husky, almost spoken bass.

sounds.name: Two-Channel Dub Sub
sounds.ref: In the style of King Tubby — 1970s dub mixes
sounds.blurb: A round sine bass for a dub, dry and deep on one side, with a thin spring echo of it on the other.
sounds.how: Oscillator 1’s sine and Oscillator 2’s triangle an octave up go through the envelope shaper together. Its output then splits: column B takes it straight, and channel 1’s OUTPUT FILTER cuts the treble for a deep sub; the reverb takes it too and sends its springs to channel 2, whose OUTPUT FILTER cuts the bass. The two output channels become two tone controls, the way a dub engineer splits a bass between a dry fader and an echo send.

steps.title: Sine and triangle through the envelope
steps.why:
Oscillator 1’s sine and Oscillator 2’s triangle, an octave up, straight into the envelope shaper, both following the keys.
- Pins D1, D4, I8, J8 and B12. Unpin D2.
- Oscillator 1 FREQUENCY 6 · 262 Hz, sine LEVEL 7 · 0.7 V, SHAPE 5: a pure sine.
- Oscillator 2 FREQUENCY 6.7 · 523 Hz, triangle LEVEL 5 · 0.4 V, SHAPE 5.
- INPUT LEVEL CHANNEL 1 at 5 · 1 semitone per key.
- Envelope ATTACK 1 · 4 ms, ON 0 · 0 ms, DECAY 5.5 · 320 ms, Envelope OFF 10 · manual: waits for a key. Envelope SIGNAL LEVEL 7 · 1.2 V.
- Oscillator 1 ramp LEVEL 0 · 0 V: the Default patch’s sawtooth is not used.
- Listen for: a soft, round bass on the left.

steps.title: Channel 1: dry and deep
steps.why:
Channel 1’s tone and place.
- OUTPUT FILTER CHANNEL 1 at 2 · treble cut: the top taken off, the sub left.
- PAN CHANNEL 1 at 3 · left of centre, OUTPUT LEVEL CHANNEL 1 at 8 · 60% open.

steps.title: Channel 2: the spring send
steps.why:
The envelope signal into the reverb, and the reverb alone to channel 2.
- Pins G12 and C14. Unpin C12.
- Reverb MIX 8 · 76% spring, LEVEL 8 · 1.3 V.
- OUTPUT FILTER CHANNEL 2 at 7.5 · bass cut: the bass cut, so only the springs’ splash is left.
- PAN CHANNEL 2 at 8 · right of centre, OUTPUT LEVEL CHANNEL 2 at 8 · 60% open.
- Listen for: a deep, dry bass left of centre and a thin, splashy echo of it on the right.

context.out1.filter: In this sound: how deep the dry side is.
context.out2.filter: In this sound: how thin the spring side is.
context.rev.mix: In this sound: the spring send. It only reaches channel 2.
context.osc2.tri: In this sound: the octave that lets the bass be heard on small speakers.

tweaks.hear: The echo gets its bass back and muddies the low end.
A tighter, more staccato bass.

sounds.name: Joystick Acid Line
sounds.ref: In the style of Ceephax Acid Crew — 2000s London acid
sounds.blurb: A squelching sixteenth-note acid bass, its filter held open a little by the joystick.
sounds.how: Oscillator 2’s square goes through the filter with RESPONSE near its peak, and the trapezoid (N11) snaps the filter open on each note. The joystick’s vertical row (16) is pinned into column N too, so where you leave the stick sets how bright the line is, the job a cut-off knob does on a bass machine. Here it is left pulled towards you, which lowers its voltage and so raises the filter.

steps.title: A square through a peaky filter
steps.why:
Oscillator 2’s square into the filter, following the keys.
- Pins H3 and J8. Unpin D2 and I8.
- Oscillator 2 FREQUENCY 6 · 262 Hz, square LEVEL 7 · 1 V, SHAPE 5. INPUT LEVEL CHANNEL 1 at 5 · 1 semitone per key.
- Filter FREQUENCY 4.2 · 122 Hz, RESPONSE 6.2 · sharp peak, LEVEL 7 · 1 V.
- Oscillator 1 ramp LEVEL 0 · 0 V: the Default patch’s sawtooth is not used.

steps.title: Short notes
steps.why:
The filter through the envelope shaper to both outputs.
- Pins D10, B12 and C12.
- Envelope ATTACK 0 · 2 ms, ON 0 · 0 ms, DECAY 3.8 · 76 ms, Envelope OFF 10 · manual: waits for a key. Envelope SIGNAL LEVEL 6.5 · 1.1 V.
- Listen for: a dark, muffled line.

steps.title: The trapezoid squelches
steps.why:
The trapezoid into the filter frequency.
- Pin N11.
- TRAPEZOID LEVEL 4 · 0.5 V: almost two octaves of sweep on each note.
- Listen for: each note squelching open and shut.

steps.title: The joystick holds the cut-off
steps.why:
The joystick’s vertical row into column N as well (N16).
- Pin N16.
- RANGE (vertical) 6 · ±1.2 V.
- Joystick (up-down) −0.4 · −40%: pulled towards you, a negative voltage, so the filter sits about two octaves higher.
- Listen for: a brighter, more biting acid line. Move the stick up and down while it plays to work the filter by hand.

context.joy.y: In this sound: the cut-off. Towards you is brighter, away is darker.
context.vcf.response: In this sound: the squelch. Past 6.6 it starts to whistle.
context.env.trapLevel: In this sound: how far each note snaps open.

tweaks.hear: The line closes down to a dull thud.
A screaming, rubbery squelch.

sounds.name: Space Rock Rasp Bass
sounds.ref: In the style of Hawkwind — “Silver Machine” (1972)
sounds.blurb: A chugging, gritty eighth-note bass on E with a buzzing rasp in its tone.
sounds.how: Two slightly detuned oscillators follow the keys through the filter. Oscillator 3 is turned up to 63 Hz, well into the audio range, and its triangle is pinned into the filter frequency (N6): the filter now opens and shuts 63 times a second, which adds a rasp of new sidebands rather than a wobble. It is the same pin that gives a slow sweep, used at a speed no LFO reaches.

sounds.name: Hi-NRG Octave Bass

sounds.name: Drooping Filter Bass
sounds.ref: In the style of Piero Umiliani — 1970s Italian library music
sounds.blurb: A round sine bass in 6/8 played on the filter itself, each note sagging in pitch as it dies.
sounds.how: No oscillator is used. A little of the trapezoid in column N as well lifts the pitch while the envelope is up and lets it fall as it decays, so each note droops like a fretless slide.

sounds.name: Ring-Mod Sub Octave
sounds.ref: In the style of Throbbing Gristle — “Hot on the Heels of Love” (1979)
sounds.blurb: A cold, hollow disco bass that sounds an octave below the keys, with a metallic shine on top.
sounds.how: Oscillator 1’s sine and Oscillator 2’s triangle a fifth above it both follow the keys into the ring modulator. A ring modulator gives only the difference and sum of its inputs: for a fifth, 3/2 minus 1 is half the key’s pitch, an octave down, and 3/2 plus 1 is a bright 5/2 above it. So the bass sounds an octave lower than you play, with a steely overtone.

sounds.name: Minimal Thud Bass
sounds.ref: In the style of Robert Hood — “Minimal Nation” (1994)
sounds.blurb: A short, dry off-beat techno bass, a triangle thud with a tick of noise.
sounds.how: A triangle and a little dark noise go straight into the envelope shaper, with no filter. The trick is in column L: the trapezoid (L11) is pinned into the envelope’s own decay time. It is most negative just as the decay begins, so the fall starts fast, and as it climbs back the decay slows. The envelope bends its own straight fall into a curve, which is what turns a blip into a thud.

sounds.name: Oscillator 3 Octave Arpeggio
sounds.ref: In the style of Tim Blake — “Crystal Machine” (1977)
sounds.blurb: A sparkling octave arpeggio that runs by itself over each held chord tone, washed in spring reverb.
sounds.how: Oscillator 3’s square, at four cycles a second, is pinned into the frequency columns of both Oscillator 1 and Oscillator 2 (I5 and J5): one source, two destinations. Its level is set so the jump is exactly an octave, so the pair leaps between low and high. The envelope repeats at the same speed, giving every step its own pluck. The two run free of each other, so the arpeggio breathes in and out of step.
